Introduction: A Sacred Refuge on the Cauvery

Nestled on the tranquil banks of the River Cauvery in Karekura, Mysore, Karnataka, the Srimad Sai Rajarajeshwari Ashram is far more than a religious institution. It is a living spiritual ecosystem — a consecrated sanctuary where ancient divine energies converge, where the fragrance of sacred rituals mingles with the cool breeze of the river, and where every stone, every tree, and every temple pulsates with a devotional frequency that is palpable to all who enter.

The Ashram was established and continues to be guided by the Divine Mother, Srimad Sai Rajarajeshwari, affectionately called Amma by the thousands of devotees and villagers who love Her. Ancient Nadi scriptures describe Her as equivalent in stature to the beloved saint Shirdi Sai Baba, and Her life bears this out in every act She performs. From feeding the hungry to educating children, from sheltering the destitute to healing the sick, Amma demonstrates that divinity is not an abstraction — it is a way of living.

The Ashram campus encompasses six consecrated temples, a sacred Goshala housing more than 300 cows, lush organic farmlands, and a community of devoted service that hums with purposeful activity throughout every hour of the day. Each temple on these grounds was not merely constructed — it was consecrated by Amma's own physical presence, her years of prayerful footsteps sanctifying the soil, her devoted worship charging the deities with living spiritual energy. To visit any one of these temples is to enter a field of consciousness that has been carefully, lovingly, and powerfully cultivated over decades.

The River Cauvery — one of India's most sacred rivers, worshipped as a goddess in her own right — flows along the Ashram's boundary, lending the entire campus an additional layer of sanctity. In ancient Hindu cosmology, river banks are considered among the most auspicious places for spiritual practice, as the confluence of flowing water and devotion creates conditions highly conducive to meditation, prayer, and inner transformation. The Ashram is therefore doubly blessed: by its founding spiritual master and by the sacred waters that embrace it.

This document is a detailed spiritual guide to the six temples of the Srimad Sai Rajarajeshwari Ashram. Each section explores the divine significance of the presiding deity, the spiritual and practical benefits of worshipping at that temple, and the particular grace that Amma's consecration has infused into each sacred space. Whether you are a devoted seeker of the Hindu dharmic tradition, a traveller curious about the spiritual riches of Karnataka, or simply a person in search of peace, inner clarity, and a deeper connection to something greater than yourself — this Ashram, and these temples, hold something extraordinary for you.
The Ashram as a Whole: An Epicentre of Seva and Upliftment

To visit the Srimad Sai Rajarajeshwari Ashram and walk from temple to temple — from Krishna's sweetness to Sai Baba's compassion, from Ganesha's auspicious energy to Subramanya's warrior clarity, from Dattatreya's ancestral wisdom to Shiva's cosmic grandeur — is to undertake a pilgrimage that covers the full spectrum of the divine. Each deity offers a different facet of the single inexhaustible jewel of the Supreme. Each temple carries a distinct flavour of grace. Together, they constitute a complete spiritual pharmacy, offering exactly what each individual visitor needs in the particular moment of their arrival.

The six temples are not isolated structures. They are connected by the invisible threads of Amma's devotion — her years of circumambulation, her daily worship, her prayers that have soaked into the very ground of this campus and made it, as devotees so often say, a place where the air itself feels different. Where the mind naturally quietens upon entry. Where the heart naturally opens. Where the ordinary concerns of ordinary life naturally subside into a background hum, and what remains is a quality of presence, of awareness, of being-here-now, that is perhaps the most precious and most elusive of all human experiences.

The Ashram is not only a place to visit. It is a place to serve. The volunteer programmes that operate throughout the year — the feeding of the poor, the care of the cows in the Goshala, the maintenance of the temples, the support of the surrounding village communities — provide an opportunity for every sincere visitor to contribute something of themselves to this extraordinary place. In doing so, they participate in the Ashram's fundamental teaching: that spiritual growth and selfless service are not separate paths but two expressions of the same movement of the soul toward its true nature.

It is, as those who know this place often say with quiet certainty, a place where one simply has to be still to experience the inner peace that is always already present beneath the surface of the busy mind — waiting, patient and eternal, like the Cauvery waiting beneath the stones of its riverbed, like Shiva waiting in his stillness at the centre of the dancing cosmos, like Amma waiting with boundless love and inexhaustible patience for each of her children to come home.
harake_nandi: Harake Nandi — The Sacred Guardian and Witness of Vows

Nandi, the magnificent white bull who stands eternal vigil before every Shiva temple, is among the most profound and beloved presences in the entire Shaiva tradition. To encounter Nandi is to encounter loyalty in its most absolute form — a devotion so complete, so unwavering, that it transcended the ordinary relationship between creature and creator and became instead a union of souls. Nandi is not merely a mount, not simply a vehicle of convenience chosen by Lord Shiva to travel between the worlds. He is the very embodiment of Bhakti — of devotion as a path, devotion as a discipline, devotion as the highest state a conscious being can attain. In him, the ancient sages saw the living proof that surrender to the Divine, when total and unconditional, dissolves all separation and makes the devotee indistinguishable from the Lord himself.

The name Nandi carries multiple layers of sacred meaning. In Sanskrit, it derives from the root that signifies joy, delight, and bliss — Ananda in its most concentrated form. Nandi is thus not merely the gatekeeper of Kailasa, Shiva's celestial abode; he is the gatekeeper of joy itself. To pass through Nandi is to pass through the threshold of bliss, to cross from the world of ordinary perception into the sanctified space where the Divine is immediately and overwhelmingly present. This is why every traditional Shiva temple positions Nandi directly on the central axis, facing the Shivalinga — so that the devotee who enters must first pass through Nandi's field of awareness, and so that Nandi's gaze, unwavering and eternal, falls always and only upon his Lord.

His form itself is a teaching. Nandi is depicted as a white bull — and white, in the Hindu understanding of colour and vibration, represents Sattva in its purest expression: clarity, purity, the quality of consciousness that perceives truth without distortion. The bull as a form represents Dharma — righteousness, cosmic order, the foundation upon which all righteous life stands. In the Kali Yuga, the scriptures teach that Dharma stands on one leg, weakened and burdened by the accumulated weight of adharma in the world. Yet Nandi stands on all four, firm and immovable before Shiva, because in the presence of the Lord, Dharma is always complete, always whole, always triumphant. To bow before Nandi is therefore to bow before the principle of righteousness itself, to reaffirm one's own commitment to living truthfully and purposefully.

As the chief gatekeeper — the Dvarapala of Kailasa — Nandi holds a role of extraordinary cosmic significance. He decides who may approach Shiva and under what conditions. This is not a role of obstruction but of preparation. Nandi understands, with perfect clarity, what his Lord requires of a soul before it is ready to receive divine grace in its fullness. He is the filter through which sincerity is tested, through which the casual visitor is distinguished from the genuine seeker. When a devotee approaches Nandi with a troubled heart, with a genuine vow upon their lips, Nandi recognises that sincerity instantly — for he himself is made of nothing but sincerity — and becomes the most powerful of intermediaries, carrying that prayer directly into the presence of Shiva without delay, without distortion, without diminishment.

It is from this sacred role that the tradition of Harake draws its entire power and meaning. Harake — the solemn vow made in the presence of Nandi — is among the most intimate and deeply felt acts of devotion in the Shaiva tradition of Karnataka and the broader South Indian spiritual world. When a devotee stands before Nandi and voices a vow, they are not simply making a personal resolution. They are entering into a sacred contract witnessed by the most faithful being in all of creation. Nandi, who has never in all of eternity broken faith with his Lord, now stands as witness to the devotee's faith — and what Nandi witnesses, Shiva knows. The vow spoken before Nandi travels directly to the inner ear of Shiva, carried on the breath of the most trusted gatekeeper in existence.

The Harake tradition recognises something profound about the nature of human difficulty and divine resolution. Life's challenges — illness, injustice, grief, failure, broken relationships, financial ruin, the suffering of loved ones — are not random. In the Shaiva understanding, they arise from the entanglements of Karma, from the accumulated weight of actions and their consequences across lifetimes. No human effort alone, however sincere, however strenuous, can fully untangle what has been woven across so many lives. What is required is divine intervention — a grace that transcends the mechanics of cause and effect. And that grace flows most freely when sought with complete humility, complete surrender, in the presence of one who embodies those very qualities. Nandi, who surrendered everything to Shiva and received everything in return, is the perfect witness for the soul that comes seeking the same exchange.

The vow itself — the Harake — is not a transaction, not a bargain struck with God. It is better understood as a declaration of faith and a commitment to reciprocity. The devotee says, in essence: I place this difficulty before the Lord. I trust in his power and his compassion to resolve what I cannot resolve alone. And in gratitude for his grace, I commit to this act of devotion, this service, this offering. The offering vowed in a Harake is typically an act of Seva — service to the temple, feeding of the poor, care of the cows in the Goshala, participation in sacred rituals — because Shiva's grace is not stored and hoarded but flows through the devotee back into the world as an act of love. The resolution of one's own difficulty becomes the seed of service to others.

There is a tenderness embedded in the Harake tradition that speaks directly to the human condition in its most vulnerable moments. When we are overwhelmed — when the burden is too heavy, the road too long, the solution invisible — the tradition does not ask us to be strong. It asks us only to be honest. To come before Nandi exactly as we are, with our fear and our hope held together in open hands, and to speak our truth in the presence of the most faithful witness in the cosmos. Nandi receives it all without judgement, without condition. His eyes, eternally fixed on Shiva, carry our words forward. And Shiva, who sees all and loves all, responds — not always in the way we expect, not always on the timeline we demand, but always with perfect wisdom and perfect care.

To stand before Nandi at the Karekura Ashram — in the sacred space consecrated under the guidance of Divine Mother Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari — is to stand at the junction of the human and the infinite. The vow spoken here does not dissipate into the air. It is held, honoured, and carried forward by the most devoted being who has ever existed, into the presence of the Lord who has never, in all of time, turned away a sincere heart.
bhairava: The Trishula of Kāla Bhairava — Shiva's Trident of Cosmic Authority

Of all the sacred implements held by the gods of the Hindu pantheon, none carries the weight, the terror, and the grace of the Trishula — the three-pronged trident wielded by Lord Shiva in his most sovereign and fearsome aspect as Kāla Bhairava, the Lord of Time and the Destroyer of Illusion. To look upon the Trishula is to stand at the intersection of creation, preservation, and dissolution — the three fundamental forces that govern all existence. It is not merely a weapon. It is a cosmological statement, a philosophical treatise cast in divine metal, and a living symbol of the absolute power that sustains and ultimately reclaims the universe.

The three prongs of the Trishula are its first and most immediate teaching. Each prong represents one aspect of the Trimurti — Brahma the Creator, Vishnu the Preserver, and Shiva the Destroyer — proclaiming that all three cosmic functions are ultimately unified in and subordinate to Shiva's supreme will. But the symbolism does not end there. The three prongs simultaneously embody the three Gunas — Tamas (inertia and dissolution), Rajas (activity and passion), and Sattva (purity and clarity) — the three qualities from which all of material existence is woven. Shiva holds all three in perfect balance, mastered and transcended, which is why the liberated soul is said to move beyond the Gunas altogether, just as Shiva himself stands apart from the creation he governs. The prongs further represent the three states of consciousness — waking (Jagrat), dreaming (Swapna), and deep sleep (Sushupti) — while the hand that holds the trident points to the fourth, Turiya, the witness-state of pure awareness that underlies and pervades all three. In this sense, the Trishula is a map of consciousness itself.

In the hands of Kāla Bhairava specifically, the Trishula takes on its most intense and uncompromising dimension. Bhairava — derived from the Sanskrit roots meaning "terrifying" and "one who sustains the universe through terror" — is Shiva stripped of all gentleness, all domestic grace. He is time made visible, the force that devours all things without exception. Kings and beggars, mountains and oceans, gods and demons — all are consumed by Kāla, and it is Bhairava who wields that consumption as a conscious act of mercy. For in the Hindu understanding, destruction is never mere annihilation. It is the necessary dissolution that clears the ground for rebirth. The Trishula in Bhairava's grip is therefore the instrument of the most profound compassion concealed within the most fearsome exterior — the mercy that ends suffering by ending the conditions that produce it.

The Trishula is also the destroyer of the three Malas — the three fundamental impurities that cloud the human soul: Anava Mala (the primal sense of smallness and separateness from the Divine), Karma Mala (the accumulated residue of action and consequence), and Mayiya Mala (the veil of differentiation that makes the one appear as many). These three impurities are the root cause of all suffering, all ignorance, all the cycles of birth and death. When Shiva raises the Trishula, he raises it against these three veils, piercing them simultaneously with a single thrust. The devotee who meditates upon the Trishula is not merely contemplating a divine weapon — they are invoking the grace that dismantles the architecture of their own bondage.

The image of the Trishula as seen here at the Karekura Ashram — towering against the open sky, silver-bright and adorned with marigold garlands, bells hanging from its prongs and the face of the Divine gazing serenely from its centre — speaks volumes beyond scripture. The silver metal reflects everything around it, suggesting that Shiva's consciousness is the universal mirror in which all of creation sees itself. The bells that hang from the trident are no ornament; in temple tradition, the sound of a bell dispels negative energies, announces the presence of the Divine, and awakens the devotee from spiritual sleep. Every movement of the wind that sets those bells ringing is, in devotional understanding, the breath of Shiva himself, reminding all who stand nearby that the Divine is not distant, not absent, but actively present — vibrating in the very air.

The garlands of marigold and jasmine draped across the Trishula carry their own significance. Flowers offered to Shiva represent the blossoming of the devotee's heart, the surrender of beauty and fragrance — the best of what one has — to the feet of the Lord. That these garlands encircle the trident rather than soften it is itself a teaching: the fiercest power and the tenderest love are not opposites in Shiva's world. They are the same reality perceived from different distances. Those who stand far from Shiva see only the terror of the Trishula. Those who draw near find it garlanded, adorned, breathing with life.

Throughout the Shaiva Agamas and the Puranas, the Trishula is described as the weapon with which Shiva destroyed Tripura — the three cities of the demons, which represented the three bodies of the bound soul: the gross body, the subtle body, and the causal body. With a single shaft of divine intention, Shiva pierced all three simultaneously, liberating the souls trapped within them. This is the promise embedded in every Trishula that stands upright before a temple or ashram: that the grace is available, that the liberation is possible, and that the force which accomplished it once is present here, now, and always.

To install a Trishula of this magnificence at the entrance of a sacred space, as has been done at this Ashram under the guidance of Divine Mother Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari, is to declare the nature and the purpose of that space with absolute clarity. This is a place where the three illusions are pierced. This is a place where time is held consciously, where Kāla does not creep in unnoticed but is acknowledged, honoured, and ultimately transcended. Every seeker who walks beneath the Trishula passes, symbolically, through the dissolution of their limitations and enters the consecrated ground as a soul already moving toward freedom.

The Trishula does not threaten. It liberates. It does not destroy the devotee — it destroys what was never truly the devotee to begin with. And that, in the understanding of the Shaiva tradition, is the highest act of grace that God can offer: not to preserve us in our smallness, but to shatter it — beautifully, completely, and forever.
goshala_volunteer: Giving Time, Hands, and Heart in Service of Gau Mata

Among the many ways in which people can participate in Srimad Sai RajRajeshwari Trust's (SSRRT) mission of compassionate service, few offer as immediate and deeply personal an experience as volunteering at a goshala — a shelter dedicated to the care, protection, and rehabilitation of cows. While the Adopt a Cow initiative allows devotees to support cow welfare financially, the Volunteer for a Goshala program invites people to go a step further: to roll up their sleeves, show up in person, and become active participants in the daily rhythm of caring for these gentle animals. It is one thing to contribute funds toward a cause from a distance; it is an entirely different, often transformative experience to feed a rescued cow by hand, to clean her shelter, to sit beside her as she recovers from illness, or to simply be present with her in quiet companionship. This is the heart of goshala volunteering, and it has become one of the most cherished and meaningful ways in which people connect with Divine Mother Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari's teachings on compassion, service, and reverence for all living beings.
Understanding the Goshala: More Than Just a Shelter

Before exploring what volunteering entails, it is worth understanding what a goshala truly is and why it occupies such a central place in Indian spiritual and cultural life. A goshala is far more than a simple holding pen for cattle. It is a sanctuary — a place where cows who have been abandoned, injured, aged out of their productive years, or rescued from neglect and abuse are given a permanent, safe home where they can live out their lives with dignity and care. Many of the cows who arrive at a goshala carry stories of hardship: some were left to wander city streets once they stopped producing milk, some were injured in road accidents, some were rescued from cruel or negligent owners, and some were simply too old or infirm to be of continued "use" to those who once kept them.

At SSRRT's goshala, these cows are given something rare in the modern world: unconditional care that asks nothing in return. They are fed, sheltered, treated medically, and allowed to simply exist in peace, free from exploitation. Running such a sanctuary, however, is an enormous undertaking. It requires constant physical labor, medical attention, feeding schedules, cleaning routines, and a steady stream of caring hands to ensure that every animal receives the individual attention it deserves. This is where volunteers become not just helpful, but absolutely essential to the goshala's ability to function and thrive.
Why Volunteers Are the Lifeblood of the Goshala

A goshala housing dozens or even hundreds of cows cannot rely solely on a small paid staff to meet the needs of every animal. The sheer scale of daily tasks — preparing and distributing fodder, cleaning enclosures, bathing cows, monitoring health conditions, assisting during veterinary visits, and simply providing the individual attention that helps identify problems early — demands far more hands than any small institution could afford to employ full-time. Volunteers fill this critical gap, and in doing so, they do not merely support the goshala's operations; they become the very heartbeat that keeps it running smoothly day after day.

Beyond the practical necessity, volunteers bring something that paid labor alone cannot fully replicate: genuine, heartfelt care. A volunteer who chooses to spend their weekend cleaning stalls or feeding calves is doing so not out of obligation, but out of love — and the animals, in their own way, seem to sense this difference. Many long-time volunteers speak of forming genuine bonds with specific cows, recognizing their individual personalities and quirks, and finding that the cows themselves seem to respond with warmth and recognition over repeated visits. This mutual relationship of care transforms goshala volunteering from a chore into a genuinely rewarding, reciprocal experience.
The Many Faces of Goshala Volunteering

One of the most appealing aspects of the Volunteer for a Goshala program is the sheer diversity of ways in which people can contribute, allowing individuals of different ages, physical abilities, skills, and available time to find a meaningful role.

Daily Feeding and Fodder Preparation: One of the most fundamental and consistently needed forms of volunteer work involves preparing and distributing fodder. This can include cutting and chopping green fodder, mixing feed with mineral supplements, and physically carrying and distributing food to different sections of the shelter. For volunteers who enjoy physical work and want to see the direct, immediate impact of their labor, this is often one of the most satisfying tasks — watching a cow eagerly consume a meal you personally prepared offers an instant, tangible sense of accomplishment.

Cleaning and Sanitation: Maintaining hygienic conditions is essential to preventing disease and ensuring the comfort of the animals. Volunteers assist with cleaning stalls, washing feeding troughs, maintaining clean water sources, and helping manage waste in an environmentally responsible way, often through composting programs that convert cow dung into valuable organic fertilizer. While this work may not carry the same immediate emotional reward as feeding or bathing a cow, it is foundational to the health and well-being of every animal in the shelter.

Bathing and Grooming: Regular bathing and grooming help maintain the cows' skin and coat health, prevent parasitic infections, and offer an opportunity for volunteers to check for any wounds, swelling, or signs of illness that might otherwise go unnoticed. This hands-on task often becomes a favorite among volunteers, as it allows for close, gentle interaction with the animals in a calm, unhurried setting.

Medical Support and Monitoring: For volunteers with some background in veterinary science, animal husbandry, or simply a strong interest in learning, there are opportunities to assist visiting veterinarians during check-ups, vaccinations, and treatments. This can include restraining animals gently during procedures, assisting with administering medication, monitoring recovering animals for changes in condition, and maintaining basic health records. This role requires more training and comfort with medical procedures but offers a deeply meaningful way to directly contribute to the healing and recovery of sick or injured cows.

Calf Care: Newborn and young calves often require special attention, including bottle-feeding, monitoring for signs of illness, and simply providing the nurturing presence that young animals need to thrive. Volunteers who are drawn to this work often describe it as one of the most emotionally rewarding aspects of goshala service, as they witness firsthand the vulnerability and resilience of new life.

Infrastructure and Maintenance: Goshalas require ongoing maintenance of shelters, fencing, water systems, and storage facilities. Volunteers with skills in carpentry, plumbing, electrical work, or general construction can contribute significantly by helping repair and improve the physical infrastructure that keeps the shelter functional and safe for both animals and staff.

Administrative and Outreach Support: Not all volunteer work is physical. The goshala also benefits from volunteers who can assist with record-keeping, coordinating volunteer schedules, managing donations and sponsorships, photographing and documenting the cows for adoption or sponsorship programs, and helping spread awareness through social media and community outreach. These roles are particularly well-suited to volunteers who may have physical limitations but still wish to contribute meaningfully.

Educational Programs: Some volunteers take on the role of educating visiting school groups, community members, and first-time visitors about the importance of cow welfare, the mission of the goshala, and the broader values of compassion and non-violence that underpin this work. This form of volunteering extends the goshala's impact beyond its physical boundaries, helping to cultivate a broader culture of awareness and respect for animal welfare in the wider community.

One of the most beautiful aspects of the Volunteer for a Goshala initiative is its inclusivity. Unlike some forms of service that require specialized training or particular physical capabilities, goshala volunteering offers entry points for nearly anyone willing to give their time.

Individuals and Families: Many volunteers come as individuals seeking a meaningful way to spend their free time, while others come as entire families, using the experience as a way to bond together while instilling values of compassion and responsibility in their children. Watching a child gently pet a rescued calf or help fill a water trough often leaves a lasting impression that no classroom lesson could replicate, planting seeds of empathy that can shape a lifetime of character.

Students: For students, particularly those studying veterinary science, agriculture, environmental science, or even social work, goshala volunteering offers invaluable hands-on experience that complements academic learning. It provides real-world exposure to animal care, sustainable agricultural practices, and community-based nonprofit management, all while contributing to a meaningful cause.

Retirees and Senior Citizens: Many retirees find that goshala volunteering offers a wonderful way to remain physically active, socially engaged, and spiritually fulfilled in their later years. The unhurried, gentle pace of caring for cows suits many older volunteers well, and the sense of purpose it provides can be especially meaningful during a stage of life often marked by transition and searching for renewed meaning.

Corporate and Community Groups: Businesses and community organizations increasingly seek meaningful group volunteering opportunities as part of corporate social responsibility initiatives or team-building exercises. A day spent volunteering at the goshala offers employees a refreshing break from routine work, fosters team bonding through shared purpose, and allows companies to make a visible, tangible contribution to a cause rooted in compassion and sustainability.

Devotees Seeking Spiritual Growth: For many devotees of Divine Mother Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari, volunteering at the goshala is approached explicitly as a spiritual practice — a form of seva that is believed to purify the heart, cultivate humility, and deepen one's connection to the divine through direct service to a being who represents maternal sacrifice and selfless giving.
The Personal Transformation of Volunteering

Those who volunteer at the goshala regularly often describe an experience of personal transformation that goes far beyond the practical tasks they perform. There is something profoundly grounding about physical labor performed in service of another being who cannot repay you, thank you in words, or even fully comprehend the nature of your sacrifice. In a world increasingly dominated by transactional relationships and digital distraction, the simple, tactile act of feeding, cleaning, and caring for a cow offers a rare form of presence and mindfulness.

Volunteers frequently report a reduction in stress and anxiety after spending time at the goshala, attributing this to the calming presence of the animals and the meditative quality of repetitive, purposeful work. Many describe developing a deeper sense of patience and gentleness, qualities that are essential when working with animals who cannot be rushed or forced, but must instead be approached with calm consistency. Others speak of a renewed sense of gratitude, noting that witnessing the resilience of rescued animals — many of whom have survived neglect, injury, or abandonment — puts their own struggles into perspective and inspires a deeper appreciation for the comforts and security they themselves enjoy.

For children and young volunteers, the experience often plants the seeds of lifelong compassion. Learning to care for a vulnerable creature, to recognize its needs without the aid of language, and to approach it with gentleness rather than force, cultivates emotional intelligence and empathy that extends far beyond the walls of the goshala into how these young volunteers treat people and animals throughout their lives.
Building a Community of Compassion

Volunteering at the goshala also creates a unique community of like-minded individuals bound together by shared values of compassion and service. Regular volunteers often form friendships with one another, developing a camaraderie that comes from working side by side toward a common, meaningful purpose. This sense of community extends the impact of the goshala beyond the animals it directly serves, creating a network of individuals who carry the values of compassion and non-violence into their broader lives, families, and workplaces.

Group volunteering days, often organized around festivals, special occasions, or simply as regular monthly gatherings, bring together devotees, families, students, and community members in a shared act of service. These gatherings often include collective activities such as preparing large batches of fodder, organizing cleaning drives, or hosting educational sessions for new volunteers, creating a festive, communal atmosphere even amid the practical work being done.

For those interested in volunteering at SSRRT's goshala, the process is designed to be as accessible as possible. Prospective volunteers can typically register their interest through the Trust's outreach coordinators, who will provide orientation on the goshala's daily operations, safety protocols for working around large animals, and guidance on which roles might best suit a volunteer's interests, physical capabilities, and available time. First-time volunteers are usually paired with experienced staff or long-term volunteers who can demonstrate proper techniques for tasks such as feeding, cleaning, or handling animals safely, ensuring both the safety of the volunteer and the well-being of the cows.

Volunteers can choose to commit to a single day, a recurring weekly or monthly schedule, or longer-term intensive involvement, depending on their circumstances. The flexibility of the program ensures that even those with limited time can make a meaningful contribution, while those seeking a deeper, sustained commitment can develop long-term relationships with the goshala and its resident cows.
A Living Extension of Divine Compassion

Ultimately, the Volunteer for a Goshala initiative represents a direct, hands-on extension of Divine Mother Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari's broader philosophy of compassionate action. It is not enough, in this vision of service, to simply believe in kindness or to donate from a comfortable distance — true seva calls for presence, effort, and personal sacrifice of time and energy. By opening the doors of the goshala to volunteers from all walks of life, SSRRT has created a living laboratory of compassion, where devotion is translated into direct action, and where every volunteer, regardless of background or ability, can find a meaningful way to contribute to the welfare of these gentle, sacred animals.

Every bucket of water carried, every stall cleaned, every calf bottle-fed, and every gentle hand laid upon a recovering cow represents a small but significant act of grace — a tangible expression of the values that Divine Mother Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari has dedicated her life to teaching. Through the Volunteer for a Goshala program, SSRRT has ensured that this teaching does not remain an abstract ideal, but becomes a living, breathing practice, carried out daily by the hands and hearts of those who choose to give their time in service of Gau Mata. In doing so, the program not only sustains the physical well-being of the cows under its care, but also nurtures a growing community of individuals whose own lives are enriched, transformed, and deepened by the simple, profound act of showing up to serve.
goshala_support: Financial Contributions: Every Gift Feeds a Life

The most immediate way to support Kaamadhenu is through financial contribution. Every rupee, every dollar, every euro, every pound that is given goes directly to the care of the animals. There is no bureaucratic layer here, no administrative overhead that absorbs donations before they reach their destination. The Ashram is a lean institution animated by genuine devotion, and contributions translate directly into feed, medicine, and maintenance.

Donors can choose to contribute in a variety of meaningful ways. A one-time gift helps meet an immediate need. A monthly recurring contribution provides the predictable support that allows for long-term planning. A significant donation to capital projects — the biogas infrastructure, the expansion of shelter capacity, the development of additional grass fields — creates lasting improvements to the Goshala's capability.

Some donors find it meaningful to make their gifts in honour of specific occasions: a birthday, a memorial for a loved one, an anniversary, a festival. A gift to the Goshala on the occasion of Gopashtami — the Hindu festival that specifically celebrates the cow — carries particular resonance. So does a gift made during Navratri, the nine-night festival of the Divine Mother, in whose honour the Goshala was ultimately built.
mother_home: Divine Mother, Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari — fondly revered as "Amma" of Mysuru — is regarded as the Divine manifest in human form. Her life is a living testament that anyone can not only attain but truly become one with the Divine, simply by embodying five qualities in daily life.

Seva — Serve the needy without discrimination. As the saying goes, the hands that give are holier than the lips that pray. Show especial tenderness toward animals; to serve one in need is to be divine to that soul.
Prema — Love unconditionally. See every person, animal, and element of nature as a purposeful gift. A mother makes no distinction among her children; neither should we.

Kshama — Forgive willingly, without keeping score. Forgiveness does not excuse wrongdoing; it frees the heart from bitterness, creates space for reflection and healing, and allows souls to return to wholeness.
Taalme — Cultivate patience in speech, action, and expectation. Like the seasons, grace unfolds in its own time — steady faith and quiet perseverance outlast restless hurry.
Sharanaagati — Surrender inwardly to the Almighty who has granted you everything. Perform your duty fully, offer its fruits to God, and the results will take care of themselves.

Amma demonstrates that one can live joyfully, honour family and worldly responsibilities, and still realise the Divine — without renouncing the world. Revered spiritual leaders and advanced souls have recognised her as an incarnation of Adi Shakti, in the form of Lalita Tripura Sundari. Further testimony can be found in the Naadi readings.

Under the guidance of Divine Mother Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari, the Srimad Sai RajaRajeshwari Trust carries out a wide range of community service initiatives — including food drives across multiple locations, the annual Narayana Seva (feeding the needy every November), free medical camps and dispensaries serving surrounding villages, and volunteering at schools for children with physical, hearing, and speech disabilities.

The Trust also maintains a Goshala in the Ashram sheltering over 300 cows, calves, and bulls — each cared for with love and given a full, protected life, spared from slaughter.
